name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 14 (PRKCG)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type SCA14

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant, slowly progressive and predominantly pure cerebellar ataxia caused by missense variants in PRKCG, which encodes protein kinase C gamma, most often affecting its regulatory C1 domain
Onset varies widely but is frequently early, in childhood or young adulthood, with slow progression thereafter
A recognised distinguishing feature is myoclonus, either axial or in the limbs, and some patients also show tremor, dystonia or later cognitive changes
Core cerebellar features are gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus
Because it is caused by point mutations, repeat-expansion testing is normal and the diagnosis depends on gene sequencing
Brain MRI shows cerebellar atrophy that is frequently most marked in the vermis
No disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive and includes treatment of troublesome myoclonus
reference.pathophysiology: SCA14 is caused by dominant missense variants in PRKCG, which encodes protein kinase C gamma, a calcium- and lipid-activated serine/threonine kinase strongly expressed in Purkinje cells. Mutations, commonly within the regulatory C1 domain, disturb the normal autoinhibition and calcium-dependent activation of the kinase and can promote misfolding and aggregation, producing abnormal signalling within Purkinje cells. The resulting Purkinje cell dysfunction and degeneration cause the progressive cerebellar ataxia, with associated myoclonus and other features reflecting the kinase's role in cerebellar circuit function.
additionalDifferentials: Other pure autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias (SCA5, SCA6, SCA28)
additionalInvestigations: PRKCG sequencing within an ataxia gene panel or exome
Brain MRI to document cerebellar (often vermian) atrophy
Testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs before proceeding to PRKCG analysis
Electrophysiology (EEG and EMG) where myoclonus needs characterisation
Screening for acquired ataxia (thyroid function, vitamins B12 and E, coeliac serology)
Detailed family history to confirm dominant transmission
redFlags: Rapid progression or early severe features suggesting an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
Prominent early cognitive decline indicating a broader neurodegenerative process
Severe myoclonus or seizures requiring specific management
Dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallow assessment
reference.prognosis: SCA14 is typically slowly progressive over decades, and many patients retain independent walking for a prolonged period; life expectancy is often relatively preserved, with disability driven by cumulative cerebellar dysfunction, myoclonus and eventual bulbar involvement.
pitfalls: Assuming a repeat-expansion SCA and stopping testing when common panels are negative
Overlooking myoclonus, a useful clue that can distinguish SCA14 from other pure cerebellar ataxias
Mislabelling early tremor or myoclonus as essential tremor or a functional disorder
Not proceeding to sequencing after negative repeat panels
Failing to provide genetic counselling regarding dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide symptomatic and supportive care for this slowly progressive, predominantly pure cerebellar ataxia, as no disease-modifying therapy for the PRKCG mutation is available
Treat myoclonus symptomatically with agents such as levetiracetam or clonazepam
Maintain mobility and safety with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and gait aids, and offer speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Manage associated tremor, dystonia and later cognitive change symptomatically
Monitor progression with standardised ataxia scales over the typically decades-long course
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and cascade testing of relatives
